item.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
item.lesson: A man in a green coat stands on a rock spur, back turned, above an ocean of fog. Friedrich's signature device — the Rückenfigur, the figure seen from behind — is a quiet piece of genius: because we cannot see his face, we are forced to stand inside him and look with his eyes. This is Romanticism's core idea made visible: nature not as scenery but as a mirror for the soul, vast enough to produce what the era called the sublime — awe shading into terror. Friedrich assembled the view from separate sketches of real rock formations in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains of Saxony; the mountaintop where they converge exists only in the painting. Largely forgotten at his death, Friedrich was rediscovered in the twentieth century, and this image escaped the frame entirely — it is now the universal shorthand for contemplation, printed on a thousand book covers about philosophy, solitude, and the individual facing an uncertain world.
item.lookFor: Notice that the fog hides exactly the middle distance — valley, roads, villages, all the evidence of ordinary life — leaving only the peak where he stands and the far summits: aspiration with the connective tissue removed.
